lessons.title: A Practical Asset Allocation Framework by Cycle Phase

body.text: Every earlier lesson in this course was really one piece of a single decision: how to allocate a portfolio as the cycle turns. This lesson assembles all those pieces, phases, sectors, duration, credit, gold, cash, real estate, into one practical framework you can actually apply.

children.text: Chapter 1 gave you the four phases and the growth-inflation grid. Chapter 2 rotated equity sectors, styles, and sizes through those phases. Chapter 3 showed how duration and credit spreads move fixed income through the same phases. Chapter 4 added gold, real estate, cash, and currency, each reacting to its own specific driver within the cycle. This lesson puts all of it side by side.

body.caption: How to lean across the portfolio, phase by phase

cells: Early expansion
Overweight; tilt to rate-sensitive cyclicals and small/midcaps
Duration attractive, capturing further yield falls; credit spreads tightening
Typically the weakest quadrant
Deploy accumulated cash into the recovery
Often still lagging due to the supply-lag effect
Late expansion / peak (overheat)
Broaden into capex, industrials, metals, energy; caution on richly valued growth names
Start shortening duration as hikes intensify; watch for late-cycle credit excess
Generally supportive as an inflation hedge, though hikes partly offset it
Begin rebuilding, yields becoming attractive again
New launches now often seed the next cycle's oversupply
Contraction
Underweight or tilt heavily defensive (FMCG, pharma, utilities) and toward large caps
Duration turns attractive once cuts are priced in, but avoid credit-risk-heavy funds
Can be volatile short term (dash-for-cash risk), then increasingly supportive
High value, both for optionality and for still-elevated yields
Typically the weakest phase, though the multi-year lag can put real estate anywhere in its own cycle
Trough
Begin re-adding cyclicals ahead of confirmed data
Long duration attractive if cuts continue
Increasingly supportive as real rates fall
Deploying, balance is falling as opportunities appear
Often still weak; recovery can lag the business-cycle trough by a year or more

children.text: One Illustrative Moderate-Risk Allocation, Phase by Phase

Take a moderate-risk investor with a neutral, phase-agnostic baseline of 50% equity, 30% fixed income, 10% gold, 5% cash, and 5% real estate/REITs. The chart below shows one illustrative way that mix might tilt at each phase, translating the table above into numbers.

body.title: Illustrative portfolio tilts by cycle phase (%)

body.text: Look at the swing in just two numbers across the four phases: equity exposure ranges from 35% to 60%, and the combined gold-plus-cash cushion ranges from 10% to 30%. Neither the equity allocation nor the defensive cushion is fixed, both breathe with the cycle, and that breathing is the entire point of this course.

body.text: Remember Chapter 1's phase-confirmation problem: you can only be certain you were at a peak or trough after several quarters of data confirm it. That means this framework works best as a gradual tilt, nudging allocations as evidence accumulates, not as a single overnight switch flipped the day one data point surprises you.

body.title: Mixed Signals
body.scenario: GDP growth has been strong for over a year and capacity utilisation is near multi-year highs, both classic late-expansion signs. But CPI inflation has stayed surprisingly low so far, and the RBI hasn't hiked rates yet. Nifty Bank and Nifty Auto are still leading the market; Nifty Metal has only just started to outperform.
body.prompt: Using the master allocation table, how would you start tilting a moderate-risk portfolio right now, and what would make you tilt further toward the peak/overheat allocation?
body.modelAnswer: The strong growth and high capacity utilisation put this close to late expansion, but the still-low inflation and absence of RBI hikes mean it hasn't fully crossed into overheat yet, and the sector leadership (banks and auto still leading, metals only just turning) supports that reading. A sensible move is to start nudging the portfolio from the early-expansion tilt toward the peak/overheat tilt gradually: trimming a little equity risk, especially the most richly valued growth names, starting to shorten fixed-income duration a notch, and beginning to rebuild cash and gold from their early-expansion lows, without making the full peak/overheat shift yet. Confirmation that inflation is turning up, the RBI actually starting to hike, and metals and energy sectors taking over leadership from banks and auto would be the signals to complete the shift toward the full peak/overheat allocation in the table.

body.title: Test Yourself
body.question: The economy has clearly entered contraction, GDP growth has turned negative, credit growth has stalled, and the RBI has begun cutting rates. Which single change to a moderate-risk portfolio best fits the master allocation table?
options: Maximise equity exposure to buy the dip immediately
Move heavily into Credit Risk Funds for the extra yield
Reduce equity, lean defensive within it, and shift fixed income toward longer duration while avoiding credit-risk-heavy funds
Sell all fixed income and hold only cash
body.explanation: The table's contraction row calls for reduced, defensive-tilted equity exposure, and for fixed income to lean toward duration (since cuts are underway) while specifically avoiding credit-risk-heavy funds, since spreads tend to widen exactly when growth is weakest, as Chapter 3's Franklin Templeton case study showed.

body.text: This framework describes directional tilts, not a formula to apply mechanically. Your own goals, time horizon, and liquidity needs should always take priority over a pure cycle-based tilt. A retiree drawing down a portfolio and a 25-year-old investing for the next three decades should not make identical moves just because they read the same phase off the same data.

cards.definition: An investor's baseline, phase-agnostic mix of asset classes, set according to their goals, horizon, and risk tolerance.
A temporary adjustment away from the strategic allocation, based on a view of where the cycle currently stands.
Periodically adjusting a portfolio back toward its target allocation as market moves cause it to drift.

body.text: The allocation percentages in this lesson are an illustrative teaching example for one hypothetical moderate-risk investor, not a recommendation for any specific person. Nothing here is investment advice; consult a SEBI registered investment adviser to build an allocation suited to your own goals, horizon, and risk tolerance.

points: This lesson's master allocation table combines every earlier chapter into one view: equities, fixed income, gold, cash, and real estate all lean differently at each of the four cycle phases
An illustrative moderate-risk portfolio might range from 35% to 60% equity and from 10% to 30% combined gold-plus-cash across the cycle, with the mix breathing rather than staying fixed
Because phases are only confirmed after several quarters of data, this framework works best as a gradual tilt as evidence accumulates, not a single overnight switch

Every specific tilt decision in the table traces back to a concept covered earlier in the course: sector rotation, duration, credit spreads, gold's real-rate driver, real estate's own clock, and cash's optionality
The framework gives directional guidance, not a mechanical formula; personal goals, time horizon, and liquidity needs should always override a pure cycle-based call
The next two lessons cover the mistakes investors most commonly make trying to apply a framework like this one, and then build a full sample portfolio across one complete cycle
